title: Best iOS App Developers (2026): How to Hire One for iPhone
description: How to hire an iOS app developer: what a package should include, App Store needs, how to brief it, what drives the price and red flags.
intro: An iOS developer builds apps for iPhone and iPad, usually in Swift, and prepares them for the App Store. A good developer turns your idea into an app that feels native, runs smoothly and passes Apple's review. Projects go wrong when the scope is vague, the app is rejected at review, or you do not own the code and accounts at the end. This guide helps you hire with fewer surprises.

faq.a: Native Swift apps feel most at home on iPhone and get new Apple features first. Cross-platform apps share one codebase with Android and can cost less. Choose based on your audience and budget.

faq.q: Who publishes the app to the App Store?
faq.a: The app should be published under your own Apple Developer account, so you keep control. The developer can upload builds if you give them a team role.

faq.q: Do I own the source code?
faq.a: Agree in writing that you receive the full source code and the rights to it at the end, and that it is kept in a repository you control.

faq.q: What if Apple rejects the app?
faq.a: Rejections are common and usually fixable. Ask whether fixing review issues is included in the price and how long fixes take.
If users log in, share data or sync across devices, you need a backend or a service such as a hosted database. Clarify who builds and pays for it.
